Policy Watch 2026-10-22

📅 Overview · 🤖 AI Agents · 💬 AI Discussions · 📚 AI Research · 🌐 Lab Announcements · ⚖️ Policy Watch · 🗄️ Data Engineering Watch

Sources: Politico Europe + Politico US | 3 new items ranked by Jev relevance | Generated: 2026-10-22 01:26 UTC

Highlights

The European Commission has opened feedback periods on two significant initiatives: the Articles 75c – 75d AI Act Implementing Act (deadline 9 November) and the Cloud and AI Development Act (deadline 11 November). Meanwhile, EU lawmakers are advancing new fronts — Socialists and Democrats are pushing for dedicated deepfake legislation, and publishers are pressing Brussels and London to challenge Meta's new AI terms. In the US, Anthropic has proposed a $1 billion threshold for AI risk regulation, echoing California's approach.

Upcoming deadlines (next 30 days)

Date Source Item
2026-11-09 Have your say Articles 75c – 75d AI Act Implementing Act
2026-11-11 Have your say Cloud and AI Development Act

News & commentary

Date Source Title Summary
2026-10-20 Politico Europe Socialists push for EU law on deepfakes Socialists are pushing for a new EU law on deepfakes to address ownership of AI-copied faces and voices. The legal answer remains unresolved, signalling potential future safeguards that could affect deployers of generative AI.
2026-10-21 Politico Europe Publishers want Brussels and London to stop Meta’s new AI terms Publishers are urging Brussels and London to halt Meta's new AI terms, with the European Commission stating Meta must comply with EU law and the UK competition watchdog summoning the company. This regulatory scrutiny of a major US vendor's terms may shape compliance expectations for organisations integrating such services.
2026-10-21 Politico US Why Anthropic’s draft bill sets $1 billion threshold for AI risk Anthropic has proposed a draft bill setting a $1 billion threshold for AI risk, mirroring a California law but repurposed to determine when government could block advanced models. The proposal signals a legislative approach linking financial scale to regulatory intervention that could influence US vendor governance.

Signals

Policy is moving on three tracks relevant to Dutch deployers of US-built AI. First, the AI Act's implementing details are being finalised — Articles 75c–75d will shape obligations for general-purpose AI models, directly affecting vendor assessments and contractual protections. Second, the Cloud and AI Development Act signals a push to regulate cloud infrastructure and AI development environments, which could reshape data locality and vendor lock-in considerations for mid-sized firms. Third, the deepfake push and Meta terms dispute show rising regulatory appetite for controlling synthetic media and platform terms unilaterally imposed on downstream users. US developments like Anthropic's threshold proposal indicate a hardening transatlantic baseline: companies integrating frontier models should prepare for tiered obligations tied to compute or capital thresholds, not just use-case risk. For Dutch advisers, the immediate action is feeding deployment realities into the two open consultations before they close.

Worth a Look

  • Articles 75c – 75d AI Act Implementing Act — Directly shapes GPAI obligations your clients inherit via US vendors; feedback window closes 9 November.
  • Cloud and AI Development Act — May redefine cloud provider responsibilities and data governance for AI workloads; consultation ends 11 November.
  • Publishers want Brussels and London to stop Meta's new AI terms — Illustrates how unilateral vendor term changes can trigger regulatory intervention, a pattern likely to repeat with other US foundation-model providers.

Together, these developments suggest a tightening of EU‑level AI governance while the US moves toward a more permissive, federally‑led safety framework, requiring Dutch firms to monitor both regimes when procuring and deploying third‑party AI.

Highlights

The Dutch DPA's €824.99 million fine against Uber for unlawful automated decision-making and insufficient profiling information under GDPR Article 22 signals aggressive enforcement of automated processing rules that directly affect deployers of US-built AI systems. The Commission's adoption of harmonised standards for high-risk AI systems under Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274 provides the technical benchmark for AI Act compliance, while the Dutch government's new guidance on AI additions in software updates gives practical procurement and functional management criteria. The AP's launch of a dedicated AI supervision directorate — though Binnenlands Bestuur notes it still lacks formal competence — and two open consultations on the AI Act Implementing Act (Articles 75c–75d) and the Cloud and AI Development Act (deadlines 9 and 11 November) indicate the regulatory perimeter is still being drawn.

This signals a volatile US policy environment affecting global AI governance norms.

Signals

Enforcement is shifting from abstract principles to concrete technical requirements: the Uber decision shows that "deployer" responsibility for Art. 22 GDPR compliance cannot be outsourced to US model providers, and the newly published harmonised standards translate the AI Act's essential requirements into auditable specifications. For organisations integrating third-party AI, the Dutch guidance on software updates with embedded AI functions effectively extends due-diligence obligations to every patch cycle — a operational burden for companies managing hundreds of vendor dependencies. The AP's new directorate, even without full legal powers, will likely coordinate market surveillance with other Dutch regulators (AFM, DNB, ACM) and set the tone for national implementation. Meanwhile, the two November consultation deadlines offer a narrowing window to influence the implementing acts that will define post-market monitoring, market surveillance fees, and cloud-service obligations — all of which will cascade into vendor contracts and internal governance frameworks.
